title: Larger teams cite newer and generally more cited references
description: Both larger groups cite newer and generally more highly cited references than solo authors. The results apply to the three groups shown, and the two larger groups have similar citation-count curves. At the same age, a lower curve in panel A means fewer references older than that age. At the same citation count, a higher curve in panel B means more references above that count. The works had at least one later work citing them through 23 November 2026. Each had at least one author listing Columbia University or an institution that OpenAlex lists under it. The curves pool the available reference links. Each reference is counted once per work that lists it, and each link carries the weight of that work. Works less likely to be sampled count more per link, and works with more links contribute more. In order of 1, 10 and 51–100 authors, both panels use 597, 624 and 477 works with the relevant information. Panel A uses 22,001, 34,531 and 43,548 links. Panel B uses 22,149, 34,613 and 43,772 [T75]. Reference age is the difference in publication years between the reference and the work that cites it. Panel A includes same-year references, excludes references published in later years and shows ages through 100 years. Panel B uses current citation totals, not totals at publication. Its scale is linear through one citation and logarithmic above one. Shading gives a separate 95% confidence interval at each value. The intervals come from 1,000 repeated draws within every original team-size group, including the largest, allowing a work to be picked more than once. The curves are observations, not model fits. In separate fits, older references became less common faster for ten-author works than for solo works, but the comparison for references with 50 or more citations was inconclusive [T76, T77]. Compare with Figure 4 of the original study [brief].

reviews.summary: The figure is readable and accurately presents the observed differences among the three team-size groups. Revise the claim, not the plot: the observed citation-count differences do not establish a difference in the fitted parameters.

issues.problem: The curves show that the two larger groups cite newer and generally more highly cited references than solo authors. They do not show that the fitted age and citation-count parameters both vary with team size. The separate fits support a difference in how quickly the age curves fall for ten-author and solo works, but the fitted comparison for highly cited references was inconclusive.
issues.fix: Keep the plotted data and marks. Narrow the report claim to the three groups shown and describe the model results separately: the fitted age curve fell faster for ten-author works than for solo works, but the fits did not establish a difference in how quickly their citation-count curves fell among references with at least 50 citations.

issues.problem: The caption is one dense paragraph, and the explanation of the shaded bands is easy to miss.
issues.fix: Split the caption into short paragraphs covering the main comparison, the sample and counting rules, and the uncertainty. Explain that the shading shows uncertainty at each age or citation-count cutoff, not for the whole curve at once.
